summary.heading: 1. What philosophy is — and what “natural theology” means
summary.plain: Philosophy is careful thinking about the biggest questions: what is real, how we know anything, and what makes reasoning good. “Natural theology” is the part of philosophy that asks what we can figure out about God using only reason and ordinary experience, without appealing to the Bible or any religious authority. It isn’t science either: it doesn’t run experiments, but asks about things every experiment already takes for granted.
summary.body:
**Philosophy** (from the Greek for “love of wisdom”) is the disciplined use of reason on questions that are too basic for any other field to settle. Three of its branches matter for this book. **Metaphysics** asks what reality is like at the most general level: what it is to exist, to change, to be a cause, to be a thing of a certain kind. **Epistemology** asks how we know things and what counts as good evidence. **Logic** studies the difference between good and bad reasoning. Feser’s book is mostly metaphysics, carried out with the tools of logic. The academic field that studies arguments about God today is called **philosophy of religion**.

**Natural theology** is Feser’s name for the project of the whole book. He defines it as the inquiry into what unaided human reason — reason working without help from divine revelation — can know about whether God exists, what God is like, and how God relates to the world. The word *natural* here means “available to our natural powers of reasoning,” not “about nature.”

Contrast this with **revealed theology**, which studies what God is believed to have revealed — for example, in scripture — and which a believer accepts by **faith**. Feser is careful about that word. In the tradition he follows, faith is not believing without evidence; it is believing something *because God has revealed it*, and whether a revelation really happened is itself a question needing rational support (he links this to **miracles** near the end of chapter 6, pages 245–246). Natural theology comes first and stands on its own: none of its premises is “the Bible says so.” That is why Feser says, at the end of his introduction, that the book does not settle which religion is true; it aims only to bring readers to the point where that deeper conversation can begin.

Natural theology is also not **science** in the modern sense. Physics, chemistry, and biology study how the physical world behaves by observing, measuring, and testing hypotheses. Natural theology asks about features that *any* physical world, and any scientific theory, must already involve: that things change, that they are made of parts, that what they are differs from the fact that they exist, that they could have failed to exist. Feser argues (chapter 7, pages 271–272) that for this reason his arguments are not scientific hypotheses competing with other hypotheses. A philosophical proof is not an experiment that might come out differently next week; it is an attempt to show what must be true if anything changes or exists at all.
summary.takeaway: Natural theology asks what reason alone — without revelation and without laboratory experiment — can show about God, by examining what any world and any science must presuppose.
summary.deepDive:
**Why a philosophical proof is not a scientific experiment.** Suppose a physicist wants to know whether a new particle exists. She predicts what her detector should record if it does, runs the experiment, and compares results. Her conclusion is provisional: a better experiment could overturn it. That is exactly the right method for questions about *which* physical things exist and *how* they behave.

Now ask a different question: *does anything ever change?* You cannot settle that with an experiment, because running an experiment is itself a series of changes — the detector registers, the physicist reads the screen, her beliefs update. Every possible observation already assumes that change happens. Feser makes this point at the very start of chapter 1 against the ancient Greek philosopher Parmenides, who argued that change is an illusion: the act of reasoning through Parmenides’ argument, one premise after another, is itself a change.

That is the distinctive shape of natural theology’s starting points. They are drawn from experience, so they are not idle armchair speculation; yet they concern what every experience includes. Feser’s four causal proofs start from change, from composition (being made of parts), from the distinction between essence and existence, and from contingency; the Augustinian proof starts from the reality of the truths and concepts that science itself relies on.

A helpful image comes from Feser himself (chapter 1, page 45): physics is like a metal detector. It is superb at finding what it is built to find — whatever can be described mathematically — but its success cannot show that nothing else exists, any more than a metal detector’s success shows there is nothing non-metallic on the beach.

**Two cautions.** First, none of this means Feser dislikes science. He uses scientific examples throughout and answers scientific objections in detail. His claim is only that science and metaphysics answer different questions. Second, people often assume that the only alternatives are “scientifically proven” and “mere opinion.” That assumption has a name, **scientism**, and Feser argues in chapter 7 that it refutes itself: the claim that only science gives knowledge is not something science could ever establish. So when someone says an argument for God is “unscientific,” the right reply is: true — and that is not an objection.

checks.q: According to Feser, natural theology is best described as…
options: the study of what God has revealed in scripture
the inquiry into what unaided human reason can know about God’s existence, nature, and relation to the world
the scientific study of religious behavior
the attempt to show that belief in God is socially useful
checks.explanation: Feser defines natural theology as what reason can know about God apart from divine revelation. Studying scripture is revealed theology; studying religious behavior is social science.

checks.q: Why can’t the premise “change occurs” be overturned by a future scientific experiment?
options: Because scientists have agreed never to question it
Because it is a religious dogma
Because it is a definition we invented
Because any experiment, observation, or line of reasoning is itself an instance of change
checks.explanation: Any possible evidence against change would itself be a change (a reading, a new belief). That is why Feser says the starting point is known through experience yet cannot be undermined by further experience.

checks.q: A friend says: “If God’s existence can’t be tested in a lab, believing in it is just opinion.” Which assumption is she making?
options: Scientism — that only scientific methods yield real knowledge
checks.explanation: The claim that only science yields knowledge is scientism. Feser argues it is self-refuting, since that claim cannot itself be established by science.

summary.heading: 2. What an argument is: premises, conclusion, inference
summary.plain: In philosophy an “argument” is not a fight. It is a set of reasons offered to support a claim. The claim being supported is the conclusion; the reasons are the premises; the move from the reasons to the claim is the inference. Learning to spot these in ordinary writing is the single most useful skill for reading Feser.
summary.body:
An **argument** is a group of statements in which some (the **premises**) are offered as reasons for another (the **conclusion**). The step from premises to conclusion is called an **inference**. Here is the simplest classic example, one Feser himself uses when explaining what intelligence is (chapter 1, page 31): *All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.* Two premises, one conclusion, and the word “therefore” marking the inference.

In real writing, arguments rarely come neatly numbered. You have to dig them out. The best tools are **indicator words**:

- **Conclusion indicators** — *therefore, so, thus, hence, consequently, it follows that, which shows that, we may conclude*.
- **Premise indicators** — *because, since, for, given that, as, after all, the reason is that*.

Feser writes in a relaxed, conversational style, and his arguments are full of these words. When he says that a merely potential coldness cannot make itself actual precisely because it is merely potential, the word *because* tells you a premise is coming.

Often an argument leaves a premise unstated because the author thinks it is obvious. This is a **hidden premise**. If someone says “The ice cream is melting, so the freezer must be broken,” they are silently assuming that ice cream doesn’t melt in a working, closed freezer. Spelling out hidden premises is not nitpicking; it is how you find out exactly what someone is committed to — and where a disagreement really lies.

Not everything that sounds like an argument is one. A bare **assertion** (“God exists,” “God doesn’t exist”) gives no reasons. An **explanation** tells you *why* something you already accept is so (“The coffee cooled because the room was cold”) rather than trying to convince you *that* it is so — although Feser notes in chapter 5 that many good arguments are also explanations.

This matters for reading the book because each proof chapter gives the same argument twice: first as a leisurely, informal discussion full of examples, then as a numbered “formal statement.” Your job as a reader is to see that the relaxed prose and the numbered steps are one and the same chain of reasoning. Once you can reconstruct an argument yourself, the numbered versions stop looking intimidating and start looking like a summary of something you already understand.
summary.takeaway: An argument is premises plus an inference to a conclusion; find the conclusion first, then the reasons, then any hidden premise.
summary.deepDive:
**A five-step method for reconstructing any argument.** Turning prose into numbered steps is called *reconstruction*. Here is a method you can use on every chapter of the book.

1. **Find the conclusion.** Ask: what is the author trying to get me to believe? Look for conclusion indicators, and check the first and last sentences of the paragraph.
2. **Find the stated reasons.** Look for premise indicators. Write each reason as a complete, standalone sentence.
3. **Number them** in the order the reasoning flows, with the conclusion last.
4. **Supply hidden premises charitably.** If the conclusion does not follow yet, ask what the author must be assuming, and choose the most plausible assumption that makes the argument work — not the silliest one. That habit is called the **principle of charity**, and it is the antidote to the straw man fallacy you will meet in lesson 4.
5. **Test each step.** Does each inference really follow? Which premise would a critic most likely deny?

**Worked example, in Feser’s territory.** Here is a paraphrase of a passage from chapter 1: “Hot coffee is not yet cold, but it can become cold. That potential coldness can’t do anything on its own, since it isn’t actual yet. So something already actual — the cool air, or an ice cube — has to make it cold.”

Reconstructed:

1. The coffee’s coldness is at present merely potential. (premise)
2. What is merely potential cannot actualize itself, since only what is actual can do anything. (premise — note the indicator *since*)
3. So the coffee’s potential coldness can be actualized only by something already actual. (conclusion)

Notice that premise 2 is a *general* principle hiding inside a remark about coffee. That is typical: Feser often uses a humble example to introduce a principle that will later do heavy lifting. Premise 2 is a version of the **principle of causality**, which becomes step 4 of the chapter 1 formal argument.

**The usual confusion.** Beginners often think that disagreeing with a conclusion is the same as having an argument against it. It isn’t. If you reject step 3, logic obliges you to reject step 1 or step 2, or to show that 3 doesn’t follow from them. Reconstruction makes that obligation visible to everyone, which is why it is the fairest way to argue — for both sides.

checks.q: In the sentence “The road is wet, since it rained last night,” which part is the premise?
options: Neither; it is a bare assertion
checks.explanation: “Since” is a premise indicator, so the reason offered is “it rained last night”; “the road is wet” is the conclusion it supports.

checks.q: “The ice cream is melting, so the freezer is broken.” What is the most natural hidden premise?
options: Ice cream does not melt in a working, closed freezer
checks.explanation: Without the assumption that a working, closed freezer keeps ice cream frozen, the conclusion does not follow. The other options are either irrelevant or a rival explanation.

checks.q: Which of these is a conclusion indicator?
checks.explanation: “Hence” introduces a conclusion. “Because,” “given that,” and “for” introduce premises (reasons).

summary.heading: 3. Deduction, induction, and inference to the best explanation — and why Feser claims demonstration
summary.plain: There are three main ways to reason. Deduction aims at a conclusion that must be true if the premises are. Induction generalizes from many cases to a probable rule. Inference to the best explanation picks the likeliest story that explains some evidence. Feser says his proofs are the first kind — strict deductions from premises he thinks are certain — not guesses about the most probable explanation of the universe.
summary.body:
**Deduction.** A deductive argument aims to make its conclusion *follow necessarily*: if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false. “Only Ana and Ben had keys; Ben was in another country; so Ana opened the door.” If the premises hold, there is no wiggle room.

**Induction.** An inductive argument generalizes from observed cases to a rule or a prediction: “Every swan I have seen is white, so all swans are white.” Induction is indispensable — science and daily life run on it — but its conclusions are only probable. (Black swans exist.)

**Inference to the best explanation** starts from some evidence and argues that one hypothesis explains it better than the rivals, judged by criteria such as simplicity (**Ockham’s razor**), fit with what we already know, and explanatory power. Detectives, doctors, and scientists use it constantly: “The muddy footprints and the open window are best explained by an intruder.” Its conclusions, too, are probable; a better explanation might come along.

Many modern arguments for God are of these probable kinds. A **design argument**, for instance, might say that the fine-tuning of physical constants is better explained by a designer than by chance. Feser deliberately does *not* argue that way. Near the end of the book (chapter 7, pages 306–307) he explains what classical thinkers mean when they say God’s existence can be **demonstrated**: the conclusion follows with deductive validity from premises that are certain, and the certainty of those premises can be shown by metaphysical analysis. A demonstration is therefore more secure than a scientific inference in two ways. First, it is not probabilistic and is not an inference to the best explanation, where some rival explanation might in principle turn out to be correct. Second, its premises cannot be overturned by future observation, because they concern what any observation must presuppose.

Two clarifications keep this from sounding arrogant. First, Feser does use inductive support as a *supplement*: he notes, for example, that we do find causes when we look for them (chapter 1) and that the world behaves just as we would expect if everything has an explanation (chapter 5). But his main case for these principles is stronger than induction — for instance, a **reductio ad absurdum** showing that denying them undermines all reasoning. Second, calling something a demonstration does not mean everyone will immediately see it. Feser insists that a demonstration can be controversial, can require hard work to defend, and can be rejected by intelligent people; what matters is whether, when all is said and done, it survives every objection.
summary.takeaway: Feser claims demonstration — strict deduction from certain premises — so his proofs are not “God is the most probable hypothesis” arguments and must be judged by different standards.
summary.deepDive:
**Why the kind of argument changes how you should respond to it.** Imagine two people arguing about God.

The first says: “The universe’s fine-tuned constants are best explained by a designer.” This is an inference to the best explanation. A fair response is to propose a rival explanation — a multiverse, say — and argue that it is simpler or fits the data better. The debate is about comparative plausibility, and it could go on indefinitely as new data arrive.

The second says: “Nothing can go from potential to actual unless something already actual actualizes it; things do go from potential to actual; a hierarchy of actualizers operating here and now cannot regress to infinity; therefore there is a purely actual actualizer.” This is a deductive argument. Offering a rival “hypothesis” misses the point. If the argument is valid and its premises are true, there *is* no rival, because the conclusion is guaranteed. The only fair responses are to show that a premise is false or that the conclusion does not follow.

That is why Feser says (chapter 7, pages 271–272) that the “god of the gaps” charge misfires against his arguments. A god-of-the-gaps explanation is always a probabilistic hypothesis that a future natural explanation might replace. A demonstration does not claim that God is the best available guess; it claims that nothing *could* account for what we observe except something purely actual, or absolutely simple, or whose essence is existence, or necessary.

**A nuance about “a priori.”** You might think a demonstration must be pure armchair reasoning. Not so. The Aristotelian proof starts from the experienced fact that things change, so it is **a posteriori** (based on experience), not **a priori** (known independently of experience) — Feser says so explicitly on page 307. It is still certain, because the particular experience it relies on cannot be undermined by further experience. This distinguishes the five proofs from the **ontological argument**, which tries to deduce God’s existence from the mere concept of God. None of Feser’s proofs works that way.

**Where people go wrong.** People hear “demonstration” and think “claims to be obvious to everyone.” Feser rejects that reading. Plenty of arguments in mathematics and philosophy are rigorous yet took a long time to be widely accepted. The right test is not “does everyone agree?” but “can every objection to the premises or the inference be answered?”

checks.q: “Every time I’ve eaten at this café the food was good, so it will be good tonight.” What kind of reasoning is this?
checks.explanation: It generalizes from past cases to a probable prediction, which is induction. A deduction would guarantee the conclusion; this doesn’t.

checks.q: Why does Feser say the “god of the gaps” objection does not apply to his proofs?
options: Because his proofs are strict demonstrations, not probabilistic hypotheses that a natural explanation might replace
Because he thinks science has no gaps
Because he admits God is only the best current explanation
Because his proofs rely on revelation
checks.explanation: A god-of-the-gaps argument offers God as a probable filler for missing scientific knowledge. Feser’s proofs claim to show that nothing could explain the starting point except God, so there is no gap-and-hypothesis structure to attack.

checks.q: The Aristotelian proof starts from the experienced fact of change. That makes it…
options: an inference to the best explanation
a posteriori, yet not overturnable by further experience
checks.explanation: It rests on experience (a posteriori), but the experience in question — change — is presupposed by any further experience, so it cannot be overturned. It is not an ontological argument, which works from the concept of God alone.

summary.heading: 4. Valid, sound, and how to attack an argument fairly (plus the fallacies Feser keeps naming)
summary.plain: An argument is valid if its conclusion really follows from its premises, and sound if it is valid and its premises are also true. If you think an argument is wrong, there are only two honest ways to say so: show that a premise is false, or show that the conclusion doesn’t follow. Fallacies are common reasoning mistakes; Feser often shows that critics commit them, or that his own arguments don’t.
summary.body:
**Validity** is about the connection between premises and conclusion. An argument is valid when it is *impossible* for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. Validity says nothing about whether the premises actually *are* true. “All fish can fly; a salmon is a fish; so a salmon can fly” is perfectly valid — if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be — but the first premise is false.

**Soundness** is validity plus true premises. A sound argument’s conclusion must be true. Feser claims his five proofs are sound.

It follows that there are exactly two legitimate ways to reject a deductive argument: **deny a premise** (and give a reason), or **show the argument is invalid** — show the conclusion doesn’t follow, often by a **counterexample**, an argument of the same shape with true premises and a false conclusion. Feser states this rule sharply near the end of chapter 1 (page 67): a critic who finds the conclusion strange cannot simply insist it is false; he has to show specifically that a premise is false or that the conclusion does not follow.

A **fallacy** is a pattern of reasoning that looks persuasive but is defective. These come up again and again in the book:

- **Fallacy of composition** — assuming that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. “Each brick weighs a pound, so the wall weighs a pound.” Critics say first-cause arguments do this (“each thing has a cause, so the universe has a cause”). Feser replies that his arguments don’t reason from parts to whole at all, and adds that not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious: if every Lego brick in a wall is red, the wall is red (chapter 4, page 134; chapter 5, pages 155–156; chapter 7, pages 266–267).
- **Begging the question** — assuming in your premises the very thing you are trying to prove. “He’s honest; I know because he told me so.” Feser answers the charge that calling causes “instrumental” begs the question (chapter 1, pages 65–66).
- **Straw man** — attacking a distorted, weaker version of someone’s view. Feser argues that the famous “Everything has a cause, so the universe has a cause” argument is a straw man that no major defender of the cosmological argument actually held (chapter 7, pages 250–256).
- **Special pleading** — making an arbitrary exception to your own rule. Critics say theists do this when they exempt God from needing a cause; Feser replies that the exception follows from the principle itself and is not arbitrary (chapter 1, page 39).
- **God of the gaps** — plugging God into a current hole in scientific knowledge as a hypothesis that science might later replace (chapter 7, pages 271–272).
- **Ad hominem** — attacking a person’s motives instead of their argument (chapter 1, page 40; chapter 7 on “rationalization”).
- **Fallacy of accident** — treating a feature that merely happens to accompany something as if it were essential to it. Every US president so far has been under seven feet tall, but that is not a requirement for being president (chapter 1, pages 67–68).
summary.takeaway: Valid means the conclusion follows; sound means valid with true premises; to refute a deductive argument you must deny a premise or show invalidity — finding the conclusion strange is not enough.
summary.deepDive:
**Case study: diagnosing “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”** This is probably the most common objection to arguments like Feser’s. Use your new tools to diagnose it, just as Feser does in chapters 1 and 7.

*Step 1: Reconstruct the objection.* The critic thinks the theist argues: (1) Everything has a cause. (2) So the universe has a cause, namely God. But then, by (1), God has a cause too — contradiction; or else the theist makes an exception for God — special pleading.

*Step 2: Check the premises against the actual argument.* Is “everything has a cause” a premise of the Aristotelian proof? No. Its premise is that whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual (step 4 of the formal argument). That is a very different claim, just as “all triangles have three sides” differs from “all geometrical figures have three sides” — Feser’s own comparison (page 40). So the objection attacks an argument nobody made: a **straw man**.

*Step 3: Check whether the exception is arbitrary.* Things need a cause, on Feser’s view, *because* they have potentials that need actualizing. Something purely actual has no potentials. The very reason behind the rule explains why the first cause needs no cause. An exception that follows from the reason for the rule is not **special pleading**.

*Step 4: Check the motive charge.* Some critics add that theists invented the “potential to actual” wording just to dodge the objection. Feser answers that this is an **ad hominem** (motives don’t make a claim false) and historically false: the formulation goes back more than 2,300 years to Aristotle.

**What this teaches.** The diagnosis never required believing in God. It only required checking what the argument actually says. That is the fairest discipline in philosophy: before criticizing an argument, restate it so well that its defender would say, “Yes, that’s exactly my view.”

**A caution in the other direction.** Fallacy-spotting can become a lazy game of name-calling. Labeling something a “fallacy” helps only when you can show precisely which step is defective and why. Feser himself grants that part-to-whole reasoning is sometimes fine (red Lego bricks make a red wall), and he argues rather than merely labels. Be as fair to critics as you want them to be to Feser.

checks.q: “All cats are reptiles; Tom is a cat; so Tom is a reptile.” This argument is…
checks.explanation: If the premises were true the conclusion would have to be, so it is valid; but the first premise is false, so it is unsound. (“Invalid but sound” is impossible: soundness requires validity.)

checks.q: Which is a legitimate way to refute a deductive argument, according to Feser?
options: Showing that one of its premises is false
Pointing out that its conclusion sounds strange
Noting that the person offering it is religious
Observing that most philosophers today reject it
checks.explanation: Feser insists that a critic must show a premise false or the inference invalid. Strangeness, motives, and popularity are not refutations.

checks.q: Someone argues: “Each player on this team is excellent, so the team must be excellent.” Which fallacy might this commit?
checks.explanation: It reasons from a property of the parts to the whole. Sometimes that works (red bricks, red wall), but excellent players can make a poor team if they don’t play together — so this is a classic composition risk.

summary.heading: 5. Necessary and contingent, possible and actual: the language of “could have been”
summary.plain: Some things exist but could have failed to exist — you, the moon, this book. Philosophers call these contingent. Something necessary could not have failed to be. Philosophers also talk about “possible worlds,” which just means complete ways things could have been. The words sound fancy, but you already use the ideas whenever you say “it could have gone differently.”
summary.body:
Philosophers use a small family of words — sometimes called *modal* words, because they concern the *mode* or manner in which something is true — to talk about what must be, what merely happens to be, and what could be.

**Contingent** means: is so, but could have been otherwise. You exist, but if your parents had never met, you wouldn’t. Lions exist, but, as Feser notes in chapter 4, if the history of life had gone differently there would be no lions, and they could one day go extinct. Contingent things come into being and pass away.

**Necessary** means: could not have been otherwise. Some truths seem necessary: 2 + 2 = 4; a triangle has three sides; nothing is both round and square. A **necessary being** would be something that could not fail to exist — something whose existence is explained by its own nature rather than by anything else. The rationalist proof in chapter 5 argues that contingent things can only be ultimately explained by such a being.

**Possible** means: could be, or could have been, even if it isn’t. **Actual** means: really is. Careful: in lesson 7 you will meet Aristotle’s **actuality** and **potentiality**, which are related but not identical ideas. Those concern the real capacities of real things (the coffee’s capacity to cool), while “possible” in this lesson concerns what could be true at all.

**Possible worlds.** Philosophers often say things like “there is a possible world in which Mars has three moons.” This does not mean there is another planet somewhere, or a parallel universe you could visit. A **possible world** is simply a complete way things could have been. Feser explains the idea in chapter 3: in the actual world Mars has two moons, but it could have had one or three; there could have been unicorns; the laws of physics could have been different. What is *not* a possible world is anything self-contradictory — there is no possible world with round squares or in which 2 + 2 = 5. Possibility in this sense is limited by logic, not by the laws of physics.

These words matter throughout the book. Chapter 3 treats possible worlds as **abstract objects** that need a ground; chapter 4 argues that contingency shows a thing’s essence and existence are really distinct; chapter 5 argues from contingency to a necessary being; chapter 6 defends God’s necessity against critics. Fluency in “must,” “happens to,” and “could” is essential equipment.
summary.takeaway: Contingent things exist but could have failed to exist; a necessary being could not fail to exist; a possible world is simply a complete, non-contradictory way things could have been.
summary.deepDive:
**Three levels of “could.”** Much confusion comes from mixing up different senses of *possible*.

- **Logical possibility**: no contradiction is involved. A talking donkey is logically possible; a married bachelor is not.
- **Physical possibility**: consistent with the actual laws of nature. Traveling faster than light seems physically impossible, though it is not a contradiction.
- **Practical possibility**: doable with the resources at hand. Walking to the moon is not practically possible.

When Feser and other philosophers talk about possible worlds and necessity, they mean the broad sense — roughly, what could be given the natures of things, and never anything contradictory. That is why he says in chapter 3 that the range of possible worlds is limited by logic, not by physics.

**Thought experiment: the contingency test.** Pick any object near you — a mug. Could it have failed to exist? Obviously: it was made in a factory, and the clay could have become a plate. Now ask whether the universe as a whole could have failed to exist or been different. Most people answer yes: the laws might have been different; nothing might have banged. That intuition drives the rationalist proof. If everything in the world is contingent, the whole collection seems to call for an explanation beyond itself — which is why Feser prefers the question “why are there any contingent things at all?” (chapter 5, pages 155–158).

**“Necessary” does not mean “needed.”** In ordinary English, “necessary” often means “required” (“water is necessary for life”). In philosophy it means “could not have been otherwise.” Likewise, “contingent” in ordinary speech often means “dependent on” (“the deal is contingent on financing”). The philosophical sense is related — contingent things depend on something else for their existence — but its core meaning is “could have failed to be.”

**The usual confusion.** People often ask, “If God can be a necessary being, why can’t the universe be the necessary being?” Chapter 5 (page 167) and chapter 7 answer this: a necessary being cannot have the features that make things contingent — parts, unactualized potentials, a distinction between what it is and that it is. The universe has all of those. Keep this question in mind; it is a good one, and the book takes it seriously.

**How it feeds the proofs.** In the worked argument later in this module, the step saying a thing’s existence here and now is “the actualization of a potential for existence” is really a claim that the thing is contingent: it has existence without having to have it.

options: The existence of the Eiffel Tower
That a triangle has three sides
checks.explanation: The Eiffel Tower exists but could have failed to exist (it might never have been built). The others are necessary truths that could not have been otherwise.

checks.q: In philosophy, “there is a possible world in which Mars has three moons” means…
options: astronomers have found a planet with three moons
Mars will someday acquire a third moon
there is a parallel universe we could visit
Mars could have had three moons: that is a non-contradictory way things could have been
checks.explanation: A possible world is a complete way things could have been, not a place. Talk of possible worlds is a precise way of saying what could have been the case.

checks.q: Which is NOT a possible world in Feser’s sense?
options: A world with different laws of physics
A world with no human beings
checks.explanation: Possible worlds are limited by logic, not physics. A world where 2 + 2 = 5 is self-contradictory, so there is no such world; the others involve no contradiction.
